summary: Defines the problem of discovering and selecting among several available access networks, and how to authenticate with them. It splits the problem into sub-problems, notes constraints on solutions and reviews the limits of existing ones. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When many Wi-Fi or mobile networks are nearby, which one should you join? This explains why that is a hard question.

questions: how to choose between access networks
how does a device choose which network to join
subtitle: Defining how devices choose among available networks to connect to.

tldr.problem: When multiple access networks are available, users and devices struggle to determine which network to join and how to authenticate with it. Pre-configuration becomes impractical as network options proliferate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC breaks the problem into sub-problems: discovering points of attachment, selecting the right identity and credentials, routing authentication requests to the home server, and discovering network capabilities. It outlines constraints on solutions and analyzes limitations of existing approaches.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC identifies the need for additional work on network discovery, identity selection, AAA routing, and highlights the risk of fragmented solutions across standards bodies like IEEE 802, IETF, and 3GPP if no unified approach emerges.

facts.label: Problem sub-areas
facts.value: 5 (discovery, identity selection, AAA routing, payload routing, network capabilities)

facts.label: Primary focus
facts.value: Identity and realm selection, AAA routing limitations

today: RFC 5113 remains the authoritative statement of the network discovery and selection problem, cited by standards bodies working on solutions. IEEE 802.11u (interworking), IEEE 802.21 (Media Independent Handover), and IEEE 802.1af continue work on the challenges it outlines. The RFC has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Devices have traditionally been pre-configured with a list of access networks and the credentials needed to authenticate to each. As wireless networks proliferate and roaming agreements become more complex, this approach breaks down. Users encounter networks they have not pre-configured yet can still connect to because their home realm is reachable. Without help, a device cannot determine which network to try, which credentials to use, or whether authentication will succeed.

The problem becomes acute when multiple attachment points within a network have different capabilities, when users have multiple sets of credentials, when multiple roaming paths to the same home realm exist with different costs, or when multiple networks are available for which no pre-configuration exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a list of all networks and passwords does not work when there are thousands of networks. Computers need to be smarter about figuring out what to join.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content: The RFC defines critical terminology for network discovery and selection. A Network Access Identifier (NAI) is the user identity submitted during authentication, formatted like an email address (for example, user@realm.example.com). Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) is the infrastructure that handles the authentication conversation, typically using protocols like RADIUS or Diameter. Roaming capability refers to the ability to use multiple Internet Service Providers while maintaining a relationship with only one.
sections.plainLanguage: An NAI is like a username that tells the network both who you are and which home organization to ask. AAA is the system that checks if you are allowed in.

sections.title: Breaking Down the Problem
sections.content:
The RFC divides network discovery and selection into five sub-problems. Discovery of points of attachment involves finding nearby network access points and their capabilities (such as security mechanisms or Quality of Service support). Identity selection involves choosing which user identity and credentials to present, especially when a user has multiple identities. AAA routing involves determining how to reach the user's home authentication server through potentially multiple intermediaries.

Network capabilities discovery means learning what services are available through a network (such as Internet access restrictions or end-to-end Quality of Service) before authenticating. The RFC notes that each sub-problem can involve discovery (finding options), decision (choosing the best), and selection (executing the choice) components.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem has five parts: finding networks nearby, picking the right username, getting to your home network, learning what services work, and handling roaming agreements between networks.

sections.title: Constraints on Solutions
sections.content:
Backward compatibility is critical; new mechanisms must work with legacy devices and infrastructure. Efficiency matters because bandwidth is limited, battery life is precious on mobile devices, and AAA servers handle enormous loads. Scalability is challenging; with thousands of potential networks and realms, mechanisms that grow linearly with the number of networks are impractical.

Solutions must also be secure. Because network discovery occurs before authentication, it is difficult to protect against spoofing. An attacker could advertise a fake network with weak authentication to trick users into revealing credentials. Management is another consideration; network devices need to provide operators with status information and remote configuration capabilities in larger deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Solutions must work with old hardware, not drain batteries, not flood networks, stay secure, and let managers track what is happening.

sections.title: Security Challenges
sections.content:
All aspects of network discovery and selection are fundamentally security-related. Since discovery precedes authentication, it is not possible to secure initial discovery using keys derived from the authentication process. Instead, solutions might rely on pre-configured information or secure confirmation after authentication completes.

One risk is bidding down: an attacker could advertise a network with weaker security capabilities, tricking the peer into selecting an inferior authentication method. Another risk is realm disclosure: if a device reveals the realms for which it has credentials in cleartext before authentication, an attacker learns what organizations the device belongs to. RFC 3748 recommends that each identity should map to exactly one authentication method to avoid these attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can create fake networks to trick devices into using weak passwords, or listen to learn which organizations a person belongs to. Devices should refuse to use weak security methods and only try strong ones.

sections.title: Major Findings and Future Direction
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several key findings. First, credential selection and AAA routing are aspects of the same identity selection problem. Second, selecting among many networks is hard if handoff latency must be kept low. Third, the proliferation of different discovery technologies across IEEE 802, IETF, and 3GPP could lead to fragmented, non-interoperable solutions unless a unified approach emerges.

The authors recommend that new link-layer designs include efficient network and realm information distribution as a design requirement. They note that a complete solution may not be possible for legacy devices on existing link layers, and suggest a phased approach: partial solutions for existing links, with more complete solutions requiring link-layer extensions. Work on IEEE 802.11k (neighbor reports), IEEE 802.21 (heterogeneous handover), and IEEE 802.11u (realm discovery and network selection) is underway to address these gaps.
sections.plainLanguage: The main lessons are that picking a network is really finding the right username, and that many groups are trying different solutions. Everyone should work together on one standard way to do it, and new network equipment should make discovery easier from the start.
